questions.text: The First Law of Thermodynamics is a statement of:
questions.detailed: The First Law says energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only interchanged between forms and shared between system and surroundings: $\Delta U = q - w$ (with $w$ = work done *by* the system).

questions.text: In this course's sign convention, work $w$ is taken as positive when:

options.label: a
options.text: Work is done *on* the system by the surroundings

options.label: b
options.text: Work is done *by* the system on the surroundings

questions.detailed: Work done *by* the system on the surroundings is positive, so it reduces $U$: $\Delta U = q - w$. (Engineers sometimes use the opposite convention; always check the one stated.)

questions.text: A gas absorbs $120\ \mathrm{J}$ of heat and does $45\ \mathrm{J}$ of work. The change in its internal energy is:
questions.detailed: $\Delta U = q - w = 120 - 45 = +75\ \mathrm{J}$. The system's energy rises because it absorbs more heat than the work it exports.

questions.text: $500\ \mathrm{J}$ of work is done *on* a gas while it releases $200\ \mathrm{J}$ of heat. The change in internal energy is:
questions.detailed:
Work done on the system is negative in our convention ($w=-500$). Then $\Delta U = q - w = (-200) - (-500) = +300\ \mathrm{J}$.

:::warning ⚠ Watch out
Sign errors dominate this topic. Fix the convention first, then substitute numbers with their signs.
:::

questions.text: The reversible work of isothermal expansion of $n$ moles of an ideal gas from $V_1$ to $V_2$ is:
questions.detailed: For a reversible path the external pressure always equals the gas pressure, so $w=\int P\,dV = \int (nRT/V)\,dV = nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$ (work done by the gas, positive for expansion).

questions.text: For an ideal gas undergoing free expansion into an evacuated space:
questions.detailed: Free expansion: no heat exchange ($q=0$, adiabatic) and the external pressure is zero, so $w=0$. Hence $\Delta U=0$. For an ideal gas $U$ depends only on $T$, so the temperature does not change.

questions.text: Regarding expansion work, which statements are correct?

statements.text: For a given pressure change, reversible work is the maximum work obtainable.
Free expansion work is zero because $P_{\text{ext}}=0$.

questions.detailed: All three are true. Reversible processes yield the maximum (for expansion) work (I); work is path-dependent (II); and with $P_{\text{ext}}=0$, $w=\int P_{\text{ext}}\,dV = 0$ (III).

questions.text: For a process at constant volume with no work other than $PV$ work:
questions.detailed: At constant volume, $w=\int P\,dV = 0$, so $\Delta U = q_v$. Measuring heat at constant volume directly gives $\Delta U$.

questions.text: An adiabatic process is one in which:
questions.detailed: "Adiabatic" means $q=0$: no heat is exchanged. If it is also reversible, the process is isentropic ($\Delta S=0$), but a real (irreversible) adiabatic process still produces entropy. Do not confuse adiabatic with isothermal or isochoric.

questions.text: For a reversible adiabatic (isentropic) process on an ideal gas, the relation $PV^\gamma=\text{constant}$ holds, where $\gamma = C_P/C_V$. This implies:

options.label: b
options.text: The gas cools on expansion and heats on compression

questions.detailed: Since $\Delta U = -w$ and $U$ depends on $T$, adiabatic expansion (gas does work, $w>0$) lowers $U$, hence lowers $T$. Conversely adiabatic compression raises $T$ — the principle behind diesel ignition.

questions.text: $2$ mol of an ideal gas expands isothermally and reversibly, doubling its volume, at $300\ \mathrm{K}$. The work done by the gas is (use $R=8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$):
questions.detailed: $w=nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)=2\times8.314\times300\times\ln 2=4988.4\times0.6931\approx 3457\ \mathrm{J}\approx+3.46\ \mathrm{kJ}$. Positive because the gas does work on the surroundings.

questions.text: A gas expands from $1\ \mathrm{L}$ to $5\ \mathrm{L}$ against a constant external pressure of $1\ \mathrm{atm}$ ($101325\ \mathrm{Pa}$). The work done by the gas is:
questions.detailed: $w=P_{\text{ext}}\Delta V=101325\times(5-1)\times10^{-3}=101325\times4\times10^{-3}\approx 405\ \mathrm{J}$. Irreversible (constant-$P_{\text{ext}}$) work is simply $P_{\text{ext}}\Delta V$.

questions.text: Choose the correct option:
questions.assertion: In an adiabatic free expansion of an ideal gas into vacuum, the temperature remains unchanged.
questions.reason: For an ideal gas the internal energy depends only on temperature.

options.label: a
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: b
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: c
options.text: A is true but R is false

options.label: d
options.text: A is false but R is true

questions.detailed: Free expansion has $q=0$, $w=0\Rightarrow\Delta U=0$. Because for an ideal gas $U=U(T)$ only, $\Delta U=0$ forces $\Delta T=0$. So R is exactly the reason for A.

questions.text: For any complete cyclic process, which quantity is necessarily zero?
questions.detailed: $U$ is a state function, so returning to the same state gives $\Delta U=0$ for the cycle. Then $q=w$ for the whole cycle — the heat absorbed equals the net work done. Individual $q$ and $w$ are not zero.

questions.text: $1$ mol of an ideal gas with $C_V=\tfrac32 R$ is heated from $300\ \mathrm{K}$ to $400\ \mathrm{K}$ at constant volume. The heat supplied is:
questions.detailed: At constant volume $q=\Delta U=nC_V\Delta T=1\times1.5\times8.314\times100\approx 1247\ \mathrm{J}$.

questions.text: Why is the work of a reversible expansion greater than that of an irreversible expansion between the same two states?

options.label: a
options.text: Because reversible work is defined that way by convention

options.label: b
options.text: Because the system does work against the maximum possible opposing pressure throughout the reversible path

options.label: c
options.text: Because heat is larger in reversible processes

options.label: d
options.text: Because $\Delta U$ differs on the two paths

questions.detailed: In a reversible expansion $P_{\text{ext}}$ always matches the gas pressure $P$, which is the largest opposing pressure the gas can push against at each instant. In an irreversible expansion $P_{\text{ext}}$ drops abruptly to a lower value, so the area $\int P_{\text{ext}}dV$ (the work) is smaller. Note $\Delta U$ is the same (state function); it is $q$ and $w$ that differ.

questions.text: $5$ mol of an ideal gas is compressed isothermally and reversibly from $10\ \mathrm{L}$ to $2\ \mathrm{L}$ at $298\ \mathrm{K}$. The work done by the gas is:
questions.detailed: $w=nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)=5\times8.314\times298\times\ln(2/10)=12388\times(-1.609)\approx -19{,}940\ \mathrm{J}\approx-19.9\ \mathrm{kJ}$. Negative because work is done *on* the gas during compression.

questions.text: Which of the following are true for an ideal gas?

statements.text: $U$ is a function of $T$ alone (Joule's law).
$H$ is also a function of $T$ alone.

questions.detailed: All three hold. For an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so $U$ depends only on $T$ (I). That gives $(\partial U/\partial V)_T=0$ (II). Since $H=U+PV=U+nRT$, $H$ too is a function of $T$ only (III).

questions.text: Isothermal compression of an ideal gas requires:

options.label: b
options.text: Work input, with an equal quantity of heat rejected to keep $T$ constant

questions.detailed: Compression means $w<0$ (work done on the gas) and $\Delta U=0$ (isothermal, ideal gas), so $q=w<0$: an equal amount of heat must leave the gas. The energy pumped in as work is dumped as heat to hold $T$ constant.

questions.text: Which of the following is **not** an expression of the First Law?

options.label: c
options.text: $U$ can be created by doing work on an isolated system

options.label: d
options.text: Heat and work are equivalent forms of energy transfer

questions.detailed: An isolated system exchanges no work or heat, so its internal energy cannot be changed — statement (C) contradicts the First Law. The other three are valid expressions of energy conservation.
